## D2. Used OpenRouter for DSv4-flash, no fallback yet needed

**What.** Probed `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` via OpenRouter; got a
clean 200 with provider `Parasail`. Stayed on OpenRouter for the
doc-study pipeline.

**Why.** Matt's instructions: try OpenRouter again first; the
2026-04-27 fallback to DeepSeek-direct was triggered by
sustained-CC-session rate-limits, not by single-call API issues.
This pipeline is many small independent calls, not one long CC
session, so the rate-limit regime should be different.

**Alternatives.** Go straight to DeepSeek-direct (safer per
2026-04-27 evidence). Rejected — Matt explicitly asked for
OpenRouter attempt first.

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. Pipeline catches per-call exceptions
and retries with exponential backoff. If OpenRouter falls over,
the script aborts cleanly and I can re-run against DeepSeek-direct
by unsetting `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` (the env-var detection in
`build_client()` already handles this).

## D4. Reframed the paper's core contribution as the "studied artifact $\hat D$"

**What.** Sharpened the contribution claim: not "doc-grounded
meta-harness," but "the meta-harness produces a *studied
artifact* before any task runs; everything downstream consumes
that artifact." Built the advisor proposal around $\hat D = (G, N,
S)$ — bipartite graph + per-section notes + hierarchical roll-up.

**Why.** Matt's textbook analogy (open-book exam, studied vs
unstudied student) is conceptually clean but operationally vague.
"Studied artifact" is the operationalization — it's something you
can dump to disk, ablate against, measure coverage of, edit, version.
This is what makes the framing falsifiable.

**Alternatives.** Keep the "study procedure" framing and treat the
artifact as an implementation detail. Rejected — implementation
details don't become first-class research contributions, but
artifacts do (cf. SkillFoundry's skill packages, Voyager's skill
library, AHE's NexAU file substrate).

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. The framing is a re-emphasis, not
a redirection — the underlying ideas are the same. If Matt prefers
a different name, the documents can be revised in 30 minutes.

## D5. Built doc-study prototype on GEOS docs (not FEniCS / MOOSE)

**What.** Pointed the pipeline at
`/data/shared/geophysics_agent_data/data/GEOS/src` — 186 RST files
filtered to 161 of reasonable size (500B–50KB).

**Why.** GEOS infra is fully wired in this repo (runner, eval
grids, treesim metric). FEniCS / MOOSE would require new
infrastructure tonight, which violates the "small-scale sanity
check" scope. Cross-tool transfer is the stretch goal for the
real paper, not an overnight sanity check.

**Alternatives.** Use a smaller subset of GEOS docs (e.g.,
userGuide only). Rejected — the full 161 files is still cheap
(~$0.20 estimated, ~10-15 min wall-clock); subset-based
prototyping risks missing the diversity of doc types (build vs
physics vs constitutive vs developer).

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. If the pipeline crashes mid-run,
partial notes are persisted incrementally and `--skip-existing`
lets me resume.

---

## D6. Subagent-style traversal via thread-pool, not Claude Agent dispatch

**What.** The doc-study pipeline uses `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`
with 8 workers calling the OpenRouter API directly. It does *not*
spawn Claude subagents.

**Why.** Matt mentioned previously trying subagents and finding
them non-performant. The right unit of work for per-section
study is "one LLM call with one section in context, structured
output" — that doesn't require an agent loop, just one API call.
Reserving Claude subagents for cases where multi-step reasoning
or tool-use is actually needed.

**Alternatives.** Spawn Claude subagents per file. Rejected —
overkill for the task and likely to hit the same perf wall Matt
saw before.

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. If structured single-call JSON output
turns out to be brittle, the script catches JSON parse errors and
salvages with regex; in practice DSv4-flash with
`response_format=json_object` is reliable on this scale.

---

## D7. Per-section schema, hierarchical rollup, global rollup — 3-phase pipeline

**What.** The pipeline runs three phases:

- Phase 1: per-section JSON note via DSv4-flash (parallel, 8
  workers).
- Phase 2: per-subtree rollup (sequential, one call per top-level
  directory). Subtree = `userGuide`, `coreComponents/physicsSolvers`,
  etc.
- Phase 3: global rollup (single call) producing the top-level
  $\hat D$ artifact.

**Why.** Matches Matt's §32 description ("hierarchically coalesce
these notes into global understanding") and the advisor-proposal
§3 formal structure $\hat D = (G, N, S)$.

**Alternatives.** Single flat rollup over all 161 notes. Rejected
— would exceed context limits (~150K tokens of input) and lose
the hierarchical structure that's part of the contribution.

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. The intermediate per-subtree
artifacts are independently inspectable. If a subtree rollup
fails, the others still complete.

## D8. Skipping end-to-end GEOS-task eval comparing studied-artifact-as-primer vs hand-engineered primer

**What.** I did *not* swap the auto-generated global rollup in for
the hand-written `GEOS_PRIMER_minimal.md` and re-run the
experiment runner.

**Why.** Two reasons:

1. **Time budget.** A single seed of one task at `dsv4` rates is
   ~10-30 min via the runner+docker pipeline, but setup overhead
   (modifying the primer-injection path, sanity-checking the
   docker mount, deciding on tasks) is ~1-2 hours that I judge
   higher-risk than just-write-up.

2. **Comparison wouldn't be apples-to-apples.** The hand-written
   primer is heavily optimized — including format conventions
   tuned for the runner's prompt template — while the auto-
   generated artifact is JSON-structured. A direct swap would
   measure prompt-format mismatch, not study-quality
   substantively.

**Alternatives.** Run a comparison anyway, accept noisy result.
Rejected — Matt asked for "small result OK" but a noisy
misleading result is worse than an honest "we didn't have time
for an end-to-end eval, here's what's in the artifact."

**Cost of being wrong.** Low. The artifact ships either way; a
proper end-to-end eval is a clean follow-up that takes a day not
an hour.
